How to refuel a spacecraft tank in zero gravity; dragonfly-shaped wings; medical AIs that change answers with the wording; the aerospace radar.
TECH RADAR
Filling a fuel tank where nothing falls: NASA simulates refuelling in microgravity
No. 12 · Monday 2 November 2026 · Aerospace · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1NASA Glenn and Case Western simulate how liquid behaves when a tank is filled in microgravity: depending on the speed, the incoming jet forms a stable 'geyser' or breaks into droplets.
2Medical AIs, GPT-5 included, can shift their cancer-staging accuracy by more than 50% just because the same case is worded differently, a US study finds.
3Aerospace radar: satellite communications remain the fastest-growing research area, and new satellite projects on GitHub nearly tripled in a year.

new aerospace papers today, few with a usable abstract
+66%
research share of satellite communications compared with 3 years ago
112
new LLM papers added to the archive today
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
Simulating how to fill a spacecraft's fuel tank in microgravity
Microgravity Science and Technology · 31 October · Free PDF  Journal
Who wrote it: Rebecca L. Winter, Mohammad Kassemi · Glenn Research Center, Case Western Reserve University (United States)
Context. Long space missions will need to store very cold liquid fuels for months and transfer them from tank to tank, like refuelling at a station in orbit. Without gravity, liquid and gas do not separate: the liquid floats, sticks to walls and can block vents, so pressure is hard to control.
The study supports an experiment by the University of Bremen and Case Western Reserve University that will transfer a test fluid between tanks in microgravity. Computer simulations, in 2D and 3D, of filling a tank with and without a vent at 1.0 to 1.65 millilitres per second track how pressure changes. They show four behaviours of the incoming liquid jet: two stable 'geysers', one low and one wobbly, and two unstable ones, where the jet sheds droplets or forms a column. A simple model also predicts the final pressure. It is today's signal because refuelling in orbit is one of the enabling steps for missions to the Moon and beyond, and this work maps the risks before the experiment flies.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · AEROSPACE
Today's aerospace papers were few and mostly self-published or without an abstract: two more below, plus one from outside the vertical in 'Also today'.
Bio-inspired flightstable
Research share −9% in 3 years · 917 papers in 2025
What it is about. Insect wings are not smooth like an airliner's: dragonfly wings are pleated. Engineers study them for small drones that fly slowly, where ordinary wing shapes work poorly.
Aerodynamics of Bio-Inspired Airfoils Under Plunging Motion
Transactions of the Canadian Society for Mechanical Engineering · 31 October  Journal
Who wrote it: Roham Lavimi and 3 others · Ontario Tech University (Canada), Stevens Institute of Technology (United States), Sapienza University of Rome (Italy)
WHAT THEY DOComputer simulations of three pleated wing sections copied from a dragonfly, moving up and down, compared with a flat plate and a classic wing profile.
RESULTThe best dragonfly section has a lift-to-drag ratio (how much it lifts for each unit of drag) 27% higher than the flat plate and 30% higher than the classic profile.
WHY IT MATTERSIt points to wing shapes that could make small flapping or hovering drones more efficient. Simulations only.
Drone applications and optimisationgrowing
Research share +17% in 3 years · 2,119 papers in 2025
What it is about. Swarms of drones coordinate by radio. Jamming those links, flooding them with noise, is one way to stop a hostile swarm, but radio conditions change constantly.
Spatiotemporally decoupled adaptive jamming for UAV swarms under non-stationary deep fading: a hierarchical PSO-PPO framework
Results in Engineering · 24 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Xin Nie and 5 others · Chengdu University of Technology, Chengdu Medical College (China)
WHAT THEY DOA two-level AI jammer: a slow layer sets the overall power budget, a fast layer decides moment by moment which channels to disrupt as the drones hop between frequencies.
RESULTIn simulations with strong signal fading, it disrupts the swarm's links far more often than four existing AI methods (from 80% to 177% better) and uses energy 26% to 50% more efficiently.
WHY IT MATTERSCounter-drone defence is becoming a research field of its own, for airports as well as conflicts. Simulations only.
ALSO TODAY
Medical AI and reliability
What it is about. AI models that score well on medical exams are being tested in clinical work. The question is whether they answer consistently.
Understanding clinical reasoning variability in medical large language models: a mechanistic interpretability study
npj Digital Medicine · 31 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Mirage Modi and 12 others · The Ohio State University, Ohio State Comprehensive Cancer Center, Ohio State Wexner Medical Center (United States) · among the authors Zihai Li, h-index 70
WHAT THEY DOThey gave GPT-5 and two medical AI models 3,035 slightly altered versions of real cancer cases, then looked inside two of the models to see how they represent clinical information.
RESULTAccuracy in stating how advanced a cancer is shifted by more than 50% just from how the case was formatted, and models sometimes gave a definite stage when the information was insufficient. The models store information in different ways, so a fix that helps one can harm another.
WHY IT MATTERSEach medical AI needs its own safety checks before use: good exam scores do not guarantee stable answers.
RADAR OF THE DAY · AEROSPACE
What it is about. Everything that flies or goes to space: aircraft, drones, rockets, satellites, and the systems to guide them and talk to them. The biggest growth comes from constellations of small satellites in low orbit that provide internet and watch the Earth.

Satellite communications
phone and internet links via satellite; still accelerating this year

storing liquid fuels at extremely low temperatures, as in today's signal

who may do what in orbit: laws, treaties, debris
▲ +25%

What developers and the public do

(year on year)		HACKER NEWS
(year on year)
«satellite»▲ +177%▲ +5%
«drone»▲ +130%▲ +19%
«rocket»▲ +50%▲ +9%
GitHub: new projects; Hacker News: stories discussed. Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025; for comparison, all new GitHub projects grew 62% and Hacker News discussions fell 38%. Wikipedia, 12 months: views down for small satellites (−39%) and drones (−25%), up for reusable launch vehicles (+15%). Research data refreshed last night; adoption data updated 27 October.
In short: Satellites and drones grow among developers well above average, rockets do not; in research the engine is satellite communications. Reusable rockets are the only aerospace topic drawing more public curiosity than a year ago.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Microgravity — the near-weightless condition in orbit, where liquids float and do not settle at the bottom of a container.
Cryogenic fuel — fuel such as liquid hydrogen or oxygen, kept at extremely low temperatures so that it stays liquid.
Jamming — deliberately flooding a radio channel with noise so that devices can no longer communicate.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the radar of the day is on energy. Worth watching: the in-orbit tank-transfer experiment that today's signal prepares; its results will show whether the simulations hold.
